title: AI Agent Red-Teaming (Tool Misuse and Goal Hijack)
summary: Red-team your AI agents for goal hijacking, tool misuse, excessive agency, privilege abuse and memory poisoning, in a sandbox that records every tool call and decision.

seo.title: AI Agent Red-Teaming: Tool Misuse, Goal Hijack | VipraTech
seo.description: Adversarial testing of tool-using AI agents for goal hijacking, tool misuse, excessive agency and privilege abuse, with full tool-call traces and fixes.

designed_for: CTO or Head of AI Engineering

problem.intro: Agents do more than answer questions. They read tickets and emails, call internal APIs through function calling or MCP servers, write to databases and trigger workflows. Once an agent can act, a successful manipulation is no longer a bad answer; it is an action taken with your credentials.

pain_points.title: Goal hijacking through content
pain_points.detail: An agent that reads emails, web pages, tickets or documents can be steered by instructions placed in that content, not only by the user.

pain_points.title: Tools with more power than the task needs
pain_points.detail: Broad API scopes, shared service accounts and write access granted for convenience turn small manipulations into real impact.

pain_points.title: Missing checks between steps
pain_points.detail: Multi-step plans, agent-to-agent hand-offs and long-term memory let one poisoned input affect many later actions.

pain_points.title: No trace of why an agent acted
pain_points.detail: Without tool-call logs and decision traces, teams cannot tell whether an action came from the user, the content or a fault.

solution.overview: We red-team your agents in a sandbox that mirrors production tools with safe test data. First we map every tool, its permissions and the credentials behind it, and identify which inputs an outsider could influence. We then run adversarial scenarios: user-driven and content-driven goal hijacking, tool misuse and unsafe parameter choices, privilege escalation through chained tools, memory and context poisoning, and attempts to skip human-approval steps. Scenarios follow OWASP guidance on agentic AI threats and map to MITRE ATLAS techniques. Every run is traced at the tool-call level, so each finding shows the input, the plan, the calls made and the effect. Fixes cover narrower scopes, approval gates, input separation and output checks.
capabilities: Tool and permission inventory with a map of untrusted input sources
Goal hijacking scenarios through user input and planted content
Tool misuse, unsafe parameter and chained privilege escalation tests
Memory, context and multi-agent hand-off poisoning tests
Human-approval bypass and excessive agency checks
Tool-call traces for every finding, mapped to OWASP agentic guidance and MITRE ATLAS

workflow.title: Inventory tools and trust
workflow.detail: We list every tool, scope and credential the agent can use, and every input source an outsider could influence.

workflow.title: Build the sandbox
workflow.detail: Tools are pointed at test systems or safe mocks, so harmful actions have no real effect.

workflow.title: Run adversarial scenarios
workflow.detail: Scenario sets for goal hijacking, tool misuse, privilege abuse and memory poisoning run against the agent.

workflow.title: Trace and detect impact
workflow.detail: Every tool call is recorded and checked against what the agent should be allowed to do.

workflow.title: Tester review
workflow.detail: A tester confirms each unsafe action, explores variations and rates severity.

workflow.title: Fix and retest
workflow.detail: We recommend permission, approval and input-handling changes, then rerun the scenarios.

inputs: Agent configuration: system prompt, model, planner and memory settings
Tool and MCP server definitions with scopes
Staging or sandbox access with test credentials

Example tasks the agent is meant to perform

Mapping to OWASP agentic guidance and MITRE ATLAS

human_in_the_loop: A tester confirms every unsafe action and rates its severity in the context of your business. Your engineering team decides which permission and approval changes to make before the retest.

faqs.q: Do you need access to production tools?
faqs.a: No. We prefer sandboxed or mocked tools with realistic test data. Where a tool cannot be mocked, we agree tight scopes and stop conditions with you first.

faqs.q: Which agent frameworks do you test?
faqs.a: Any framework, because we test behaviour through tool calls and outcomes. Our background includes building supervisor-style multi-agent systems with function calling and MCP tool servers, so we know where these designs tend to break.

faqs.q: What fixes do you usually recommend?
faqs.a: Narrower tool scopes and per-user credentials, human approval for high-impact actions, clear separation of instructions from untrusted content, checks before tools run, and logging that ties each action to its trigger.
It can be, but agents change often. Most teams keep the scenario set and run it in CI whenever prompts, tools or models change.
